content: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are a significant global health issue, affecting hundreds of millions of people annually. These infections, many of which are preventable, occur during the delivery of care in healthcare facilities and were not present or incubating at the time of admission. HAIs can also affect healthcare workers, visitors, and family members. They are often caused by microorganisms resistant to commonly used antibiotics, such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), which increases the risk of mortality by 50% compared to non-resistant strains. Common HAIs include infections of the urinary tract, respiratory system, bloodstream, and surgical wounds. The prevention of HAIs is critical, as they lead to unnecessary deaths, prolonged hospital stays, long-term disabilities, and increased antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Effective infection prevention and control (IPC) measures are essential to reduce the burden of HAIs. IPC is a practical, evidence-based approach aimed at protecting patients and healthcare workers from avoidable infections. It requires coordinated action at all levels of the healthcare system, from policymakers to facility managers, healthcare workers, and patients. Key determinants of HAIs include the inappropriate use of invasive devices and antibiotics, high-risk diagnostic or therapeutic procedures, immunosuppression, and substandard application of IPC precautions. In resource-limited settings, additional factors such as poor water and sanitation, insufficient equipment, understaffing, overcrowding, and lack of IPC guidelines exacerbate the problem. Globally, 1 in 10 patients is affected by HAIs, with higher rates in developing countries. In intensive care units, up to 30% of patients in high-income countries and 2–3 times more in developing countries acquire at least one HAI. Unsafe injection practices, such as the reuse of syringes and needles, contribute significantly to the spread of infections. Hand hygiene is a cornerstone of IPC, yet 61% of healthcare workers fail to adhere to recommended practices. In neonatal care, infections account for 4–56% of all neonatal deaths, while in maternal care, up to 20% of women in Africa develop wound infections after cesarean sections. The implementation of IPC best practices has been shown to significantly reduce HAIs and associated harm. For example, improving hand hygiene can reduce pathogen transmission in healthcare settings by 50%. Surveillance and strong IPC programs have led to reductions in central line-associated bloodstream infections, surgical site infections, and MRSA bacteremia in various countries. In Australia, sustained efforts achieved 80% compliance with hand hygiene practices nationwide. The World Health Organization (WHO) has played a pivotal role in advancing IPC through initiatives such as the Clean Care is Safer Care program and the SAVE LIVES: Clean Your Hands campaign. These efforts have raised awareness, driven policy changes, and supported the implementation of IPC strategies globally. WHO's IPC Global Unit continues to provide technical guidance, develop evidence-based recommendations, and support countries in strengthening their IPC programs. Preventing infections at the source reduces the need for antibiotics, thereby mitigating the risk of AMR. Strong IPC measures are essential for achieving quality healthcare delivery, ensuring patient and healthcare worker safety, and supporting global health goals. The vision of IPC is to protect lives by reducing infections and revolutionizing the way IPC is integrated into healthcare systems worldwide.
